stories.brief: When her mobile bill rises, Yael asks a customer-service representative to help her understand whether a different plan would suit her better. She explains that she mostly uses messaging and maps, but sometimes watches videos while traveling. The representative compares her recent data use with two plans and clarifies that the cheaper one has a smaller data allowance, while extra data costs more. Yael asks whether she can change plans again later and learns she can review it after a month. She chooses the middle option, confirms the monthly price and start date, and leaves knowing what to check on her next bill.

Before ordering new glasses, Amir asks his friend Roni to give an honest opinion while he tries on a few frames at an optician. Amir likes a bold pair, but Roni says the color draws attention away from his face; Amir explains that he wants something different from his old glasses, not just another neutral pair. They compare two lighter frames and check how each looks from the side as well as straight on. Amir asks which pair seems comfortable for everyday wear, and Roni points out that one sits more securely when Amir smiles. Amir chooses that pair, confirms the price and fitting details with the optician, and feels good about a style that still looks like him.

In the courtyard, dog owner Neta asks her neighbor Gil if he can help her practice greeting visitors with her excitable dog, Moka. Gil agrees, and Neta explains that she wants Moka to stay calm rather than jump up when someone comes in. On their first try, Moka rushes toward Gil, so Neta pauses and asks him to wait until the dog settles. Gil checks whether he should offer a hand for Moka to sniff, and Neta suggests keeping a little space instead. They try again, rewarding Moka for sitting before Gil comes closer. After several calmer greetings, Neta thanks Gil, and they agree she will keep practicing with short visits.

stories.brief: AI-generated dialogue. Neighbors Hila and Omer chat in their shared courtyard after Hila brings out a pot of fresh mint. They decide to organize a relaxed herb-tasting afternoon for a few residents, and Omer asks whether it should be a formal event or an informal drop-in. Hila prefers something simple, but clarifies that they should offer more than mint tea. They compare ideas such as lemon water and small herb spreads, then discuss how to make the tasting comfortable for people who do not eat certain foods. Omer asks who will bring cups and serving plates; Hila suggests asking each neighbor to bring one small item, while she prepares a list of ingredients. They agree on a weekend afternoon, a modest menu, and a short message inviting everyone to share a favorite herb or recipe.

stories.brief: AI-generated dialogue. Siblings Maya and Erez want to make a shared digital album of family photos from recent gatherings, but they need to agree on what to include and who can see it. Maya suggests adding every photo from their phones, while Erez asks whether that would make the album hard to browse. They decide to choose a small set together and clarify that private or unflattering pictures should stay out unless the person in them agrees. Erez asks whether their parents should be able to add photos too; Maya likes the idea but wants to show them how first. They discuss naming the album by year and adding short captions for places and occasions. Erez offers to create it, Maya volunteers to select the first photos, and they agree to share the finished album with close family only.

stories.brief: A collection of independent short practical situations from ordinary daily life.

shortItems.brief: At the post office, a customer asks which counter accepts prepaid parcels. The clerk points to the marked drop-off desk, and the customer leaves the parcel there.
A passenger asks the bus driver whether the next stop is called Oak Street. The driver confirms it, and the passenger gets ready to step off.
When the power briefly flickers, one housemate asks another to borrow a flashlight. The other finds one in the hall cupboard, and the housemate uses it to see clearly.
A shopper asks an electronics store employee whether a small alarm clock comes with batteries. The employee says it does not, so the shopper adds the correct batteries to the basket.
A new employee asks a coworker how to reserve a desk for tomorrow. The coworker shows them the booking calendar, and the employee reserves an open desk.
At a friend's house, a guest asks where the board games are kept. The host brings out a short card game, and they begin playing at the table.
A home cook asks a housemate what temperature to set for baking a tray of vegetables. The housemate checks the recipe, and the cook sets the oven to the listed temperature.
A phone user asks a friend how to turn on captions for a video. The friend points out the captions setting, and the user switches it on.

A visitor at a community sports center asks the front desk for a bandage after getting a small paper cut. The staff member hands one over, and the visitor covers the cut before returning to the activity.
A customer at a shoe shop asks whether there is a shoehorn to help try on a pair of boots. The employee brings one over, and the customer slips the boots on comfortably.
A walker in a botanical garden asks a groundskeeper whether there is a bench near the pond. The groundskeeper points along the path, and the walker finds a shaded place to rest.

Bungo, the Tel Aviv zoo’s first elephant, arrived in Haifa in 1946; children’s poet Leah Goldberg followed his journey in a series of poems and stories.

sources.title: The Trials and Tribulations of the First Hebrew Elephant
New Elephant at Tel Aviv Zoo

storyBeats: Tel Aviv children repeatedly asked zoo director Baruch Goffer why their zoo had no elephant. Earlier attempts to obtain one from India had run into bureaucratic obstacles.
Bungo was born in the Belgian Congo. The National Library account says his birth name was Bungo, while the Hebrew account gives it as Bangdi and says people called him Bango.
Getting Bungo into the ship’s large transport crate required feeding him a very large quantity of bananas.

Leah Goldberg, the resident poet of the children’s newspaper Davar LaYeladim, began a series called “The Great Journey” about Bungo’s voyage and arrival. Its first installment appeared on October 24, 1946.
Bungo reached Haifa on October 30, 1946. Zoo director Goffer later recalled finding him in the crate aboard the ship and seeing him raise his trunk toward the visitors.
Goldberg published another installment of “The Great Journey” as Bungo entered the zoo; it appeared in Davar LaYeladim on October 31, 1946.

The arrival drew broad press coverage and large crowds eager to see the elephant. The National Library’s newspaper collection includes a November 1, 1946 issue of The Palestine Post, which reported on the event.
A 1947 color film preserved by the Steven Spielberg Jewish Film Archive shows Bungo at the Tel Aviv Zoo.
Bungo was kept alone at first. Goffer described episodes in which he overturned a keeper’s wheelbarrow and ran off with the keeper’s broom and tools before calming down.

About a year later, a younger, smaller elephant named Magumba arrived as Bungo’s companion. Goffer described the two eating together, and Goldberg’s children’s newspaper continued to feature their story.
Bungo lived at the Tel Aviv Zoo until his death in 1960.

stories.brief: Music researcher and teacher Abraham Zvi Idelsohn set new Hebrew words to an older Hasidic melody, creating the song “Hava Nagila.”

sources.title: Where Allenby Meets Balfour – The Birth of Hava Nagila

storyBeats: Abraham Zvi Idelsohn was a cantor, music teacher, composer, and researcher of Jewish music. He collected and documented melodies from Jewish communities and traditions.
The melody later used for “Hava Nagila” was a wordless Hasidic tune that Idelsohn heard in Jerusalem from Sadigura Hasidim in 1915.
The British capture of Jerusalem in December 1917 and the Balfour Declaration of November 1917 were followed by public celebrations and new songs in the Jewish community of Jerusalem.
In 1918, Idelsohn sought a popular tune for his mixed choir in Jerusalem and chose the Hasidic melody, setting Hebrew words to it and arranging it for four voices.
The song’s Hebrew text calls for rejoicing and singing, and includes the call for brothers to rise with joyful hearts. The National Library connects its wording to Psalm 118:24.

The National Library account says Idelsohn’s choir performed the song in Jerusalem, where the audience received it warmly; it was sung in the streets the following day and soon spread beyond the city.
Idelsohn’s ten-volume collection, Otzar Neginot Yisrael, published between 1914 and 1932, documented Jewish musical traditions from different communities.
Idelsohn recorded “Hava Nagila” with a men’s choir in Berlin in 1922 for the German Polydor label, giving the song an early commercial recording.
Idelsohn’s adaptation retained an older Hasidic melody but changed its role by pairing it with new Hebrew words and a choral arrangement.

stories.brief: The ATA textile factory operated in Kiryat Ata from 1934 to 1985, producing clothing and household textiles sold across Israel, including in its own chain of stores.

sources.title: Labour relations in Israel: A case study of ATA
The “Ata” Textile Co.: Fourth process in the spinning of the yarn

storyBeats: The Moller family, Jewish textile industrialists from Czechoslovakia, established the ATA textile factory at Kfar Ata in 1934.
Before construction, the factory project involved buying land, drilling for water, building a connecting road, ordering factory buildings in Europe, and training workers.
The factory made clothing and textiles for industrial and household use. Its products were sold across Israel through private businesses and its own chain of stores.
A 1934–1939 Library of Congress photograph documents one stage of yarn spinning at the ATA factory near Acre, identifying the site as Kfar-Ata.
During the Second World War, ATA became the largest supplier of clothing to the British army in the Middle East, according to the CET historical account.
After Israel was established, ATA became a major supplier of clothing to civilian and military sectors, according to the same historical account.
The International Labour Organization’s 1955 case study describes ATA as having two factories, its own marketing organization, and about 1,500 employees, 27 percent of them women.
The ILO report describes a central workers’ committee with elected representatives from factory departments and annual collective-agreement negotiations with the Haifa Labour Council.
A wage dispute led to a strike in 1949. The ILO account says the matter was settled with the help of an arbitrator from the Ministry of Labour’s Labour Relations Division.

The factory archive includes records and materials on company history, social life, textile and clothing products, design sketches, marketing, and press coverage; some items were donated by the founders’ sons and veteran workers.

The factory closed in May 1985 after financial and management difficulties, according to CET’s historical account. The site was later redeveloped, while the water tower remained as a visible factory remnant.
